title: Two are better than one (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12)
hookLine: if one falls, the other lifts; a threefold cord is not quickly broken

cards: Right before today's passage, the Preacher describes a man who has no one: no child, no brother. There's no end to his work, the text says, and his eyes are never satisfied with his money.

He never stops to ask who all this is for. It's a sharp little portrait, and it could be someone you know: the one who answers emails at midnight, eats at the desk, and hasn't called a friend in a year.
The Preacher has looked hard at everything under the sun and found most of it breath. But in the middle of all that hevel, he finds something that holds.

teach.h: A MAN ALONE, WORKING FOR NO ONE.
teach.b: The King James Bible: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Then the Preacher gives three pictures, all very physical.
First, the fall: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." A road at night, a ditch, a twisted ankle.

teach.h: IF ONE FALLS, THE OTHER LIFTS.
teach.b: Second, the cold: two lying together keep each other warm, but how can one be warm alone?

teach.h: TWO KEEP WARM; TWO STAND FIRM.
teach.b: Third, the attack: someone might overpower a person alone, but two can stand against him. Fall, cold, danger. Each time, a second person is the difference.

Then, almost as a proverb tacked on the end, the line your carry comes from: "and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Twist two strands together and they're stronger. Twist in a third and the rope holds far more.
The Preacher counted two, and then the proverb says three. Readers have wondered about that. At Christian weddings, the third strand is often heard as God, woven in with the couple.
Others hear it simply as a proverb about community: two is good, more is better. The text itself doesn't say who the third strand is.
But here's the striking thing: the Preacher who called everything breath doesn't call friendship breath. In a book that doubts almost everything, he's sure of this.

how: Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 is a common reading at Christian weddings, where the threefold cord is often explained as husband, wife and God; some couples braid three cords during the ceremony.

o: the lonely worker whose eyes are never satisfied with money
a cord of three strands that is not quickly broken
breath or vapor, the Preacher's word for what doesn't last

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: the passage says the third strand is God
the text doesn't say. at Christian weddings it's often heard as God; others hear community.
the Preacher, who calls most things breath, holds onto friendship here
in a book that doubts almost everything, two are better than one.
the passage was written for weddings
it's about companionship of every kind: falls, cold nights, danger on the road.

games.q: you're traveling alone at night and fall into a ditch. what does the Preacher say about this moment?
o: climb out yourself: that's what strength is.
woe to the one who is alone, with no one to help him up.
falling is just breath, so it doesn't matter.
games.why: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." the Preacher's answer to a fall is a friend.

practice: Bring to mind someone who once lifted you when you fell, a hard week, a bad diagnosis, a breakup, a day you couldn't get off the couch, and remember one specific thing they did: the call, the meal, the ride, the hour they just sat there.
Notice how that time might have gone alone, and find the plain words you'd use to thank them. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Hevel. The Preacher's word for breath or vanity, used throughout Ecclesiastes for what doesn't last, except, he says, for a friend who helps you up.

orig.note: Hebrew: the threefold cord, a thread twisted from three strands.

carryVoice: Your line: a threefold cord. Two strands hold, and a third holds more. Day four hundred fifty-six.
